framework: LangChain; MetaGPT; AutoGen; CAMEL; CrewAI; LangGraph
failure_observed: A single atomic false claim (endogenous seed or injected message) spreads through message dependencies until agents converge on a false consensus.
locus_detail: tracer seed planted in the entry agent system instructions (endogenous probe); application-layer injected messages from an external adversary (attack)
evaluation: QUANT/RIGID/MMLU scenarios; S(t) coverage, ASR, BICR, safe completion, token cost; six frameworks in chain/star/mesh topologies; baselines AGrail, CFG, Reflection; GPT-4o-mini for decomposition
limitation: Binary adoption variable may miss partial internalization; injection study is a controlled probe, not full adversarial behavior.
evidence_note: trigger: endogenous seed "solely employed for measuring endogenous vulnerabilities" (§IV-A) plus Compliance/Security-FUD injection attacks (§V, §VII-B); trigger_evidence_level: benign seed set in system instructions of entry agent, attack injected as application-layer messages, different interface so both-different-locus; locus: seed in "system-level instructions of the entry agent" (§IV-A), "injected messages" (§III); spread: S(t) fraction of agents adopting seed per message step, Fig. 4 (reach, so cascades not amplifies); defense_family: genealogy governance layer detects/blocks/repairs claims at message layer (§VI); defense_evaluated_against: Table V reports BICR under Baseline/Compliance/Security FUD attacks only, no clean-run or endogenous test of the defense
review_note: Abstract says defense handles endogenous and exogenous errors; only attack settings appear in defense Table V. Code/data link is anonymous, traces not stated so trace_release=no.

failure_observed: Adversarial content accepted at one inter-agent boundary (retrieved content, plan, consensus, identity) is forwarded as trusted input and corrupts the pipeline output.
locus_detail: retrieved content into a retrieval agent; planner decomposition and sub-agent results accepted by the orchestrator; Sybil agent at a routing slot
evaluation: 147 annotated TRAIL traces (GAIA, SWE-Bench Lite); 1,080 attack runs plus 90 clean runs on a 10-agent five-layer pipeline; ASR, accuracy, recovery rate, hop count; GPT-5-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Kimi K2.5
limitation: Reviewer: defenses (attestation, quorum, auditing) are only argued, not implemented or tested; one pipeline design.
evidence_note: trigger: benign failures from TRAIL production traces (§III) plus injected attacks A1-A4 on a separate simulated pipeline (§IV); trigger_evidence_level: trace analysis on GAIA/SWE-Bench agents, attacks on a custom 10-agent pipeline, different systems; locus: A1 retrieved content, A2 sub-agent results to orchestrator, A3 planner, A4 routing slot (§III); spread: hop count 4-6 under A1/A2, Fig. 6d; defense_family: none implemented, mitigations only discussed (§V)
review_note: Paper names attacks but the vulnerability classes come from benign traces; abstract says vulnerabilities arise in benign deployments. Pipeline vs hierarchy is a close call (orchestrator plus layers); chose pipeline as the paper does.

framework: ChatDev; MetaGPT; HyperAgent; AppWorld; AG2; Magentic-One; OpenManus
failure_observed: MAS fail through specification and role violations, inter-agent misalignment (ignored input, withheld information, reasoning-action mismatch) and missing or incorrect verification.
locus_detail: agents disobeying task or role specifications; inter-agent misalignment in conversation; verifier agents
evaluation: 1642 annotated traces from 7 MAS frameworks (ProgramDev, SWE-Bench Lite, GAIA, GSM-Plus, OlympiadBench, MMLU); failure-mode prevalence, kappa; GPT-4o, Claude 3.7, Qwen2.5, CodeLlama
limitation: Authors state MAST does not claim to cover every potential failure pattern; interventions leave many failure modes unresolved.
evidence_note: trigger: failures = "instances where the MAS does not achieve its intended task objectives", no adversary (§1); trigger_evidence_level: no attacks anywhere in the paper; locus: failure modes 1.1/1.2 disobey spec, 2.x inter-agent misalignment (Fig. 1); spread: taxonomy gives prevalence per mode, no measure of movement between agents; defense_family: added task-verification step in ChatDev, +15.6% task success (§5, App. H); defense_evaluated_against: intervention case studies measure task success on benign runs only (App. H)
review_note: Defense coding rests on the two appendix intervention case studies (role-spec rewrite, added verification step), not a proposed defense method; reviewer may prefer none. Mechanism primary is a judgment among 14 modes.

framework: MetaGPT; Self-collab; Camel; SPP; MAD; AgentVerse
failure_observed: A clumsy or malicious agent that introduces stealthy errors lowers task performance, by different amounts in linear, flat and hierarchical structures.
locus_detail: one faulty agent per run, made faulty by profile rewriting (AutoTransform) or by message error injection (AutoInject)
evaluation: Code generation, math, translation, text evaluation (HumanEval, CIAR, CommonMT, FairEval); performance drop; six systems of 2-5 agents; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o
limitation: Shared GPT-3.5/GPT-4o backbones and automatic scores only; structure effects entangled with each framework prompt design.
evidence_note: trigger: AutoTransform rewrites a profile to produce "stealthy errors" (instructed sabotage) and AutoInject inserts errors into messages (injected fault) (§3); trigger_evidence_level: both applied to the same faulty-agent role in the same six systems and compared directly (§4, Table 1); locus: one faulty agent at a time, profile vs message interface (§3, §4.1); defense_family: Challenger adds challenge ability to profiles, Inspector is an extra reviewing agent (§5); defense_evaluated_against: Table 3 under both AutoTransform and AutoInject, recovering up to 96.4%; spread: only performance drop per structure in main text, App. B.3-B.4 mention propagation in passing
review_note: trigger is a judgment call: AutoTransform instructs an agent to insert hidden errors (adversarial by the sabotage rule) while AutoInject is an injected error (benign by rule); the paper calls both clumsy or malicious. If a reviewer treats both as fault simulation the row becomes benign-bug/benign-only/benign.

failure_observed: Byzantine (weaker-model) agents in a graph of LLM agents drive consensus to wrong answers in math reasoning and safety assessment tasks.
locus_detail: Byzantine agents (GPT-3.5-turbo) placed at random, central or leaf nodes of chain, tree, star, complete, random and layered graphs
evaluation: GSM8K and XSTest (plus CommonsenseQA in appendix), 10 questions each; round-level accuracy, BFT improvement; 7-node graphs with 1-6 Byzantine nodes; GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-3.5-turbo
limitation: Small question sets (10 per task); multi-round consensus is costly; confidence probes need training data.
evidence_note: trigger: "Malicious/Byzantine Agent: OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo" versus honest GPT-4o-mini, no instruction to deceive (App. A, Experimental Setting); trigger_evidence_level: only weak-model Byzantine nodes appear; locus: Byzantine nodes placed by position in each topology (App. A.3); spread: only final accuracy per topology and malicious count, no movement measure; defense_family: CP-WBFT confidence-weighted consensus aggregation (Methods); defense_evaluated_against: CP-WBFT tested only with the weak-model Byzantine setting (Table 2, Experimental Setting)
review_note: Paper calls the weak-model agents malicious; coded benign-bug by the how-induced rule.

failure_observed: A malicious prompt in external content hijacks one agent and self-replicates through agent-to-agent messages, causing data theft, scams, malware spread or disruption.
locus_detail: injection in a document, email or web page read by the first tool agent, then relayed by agent messages (global or local messaging)
evaluation: 120 instructions x attack types (360 pairs) for data theft, scams, content manipulation, malware; society of 10-50 agents; ASR, infected-agent counts; GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 Turbo
limitation: Mostly GPT models; basic architectures; LLM Tagging tested with handcrafted rather than adaptive attacks.
evidence_note: trigger: malicious prompts embedded in external content (§4.1); trigger_evidence_level: no benign condition; locus: infection embedded in PDF/email/web content then passed agent to agent (§4.1); spread: infected-agent counts over turns for 10-50 agents, Fig. 6; defense_family: LLM Tagging marks agent-origin messages, combined with marking, instruction and sandwich prompt defenses (§6); defense_evaluated_against: Fig. 7 attack success rate with and without tagging, attacks only
review_note: Society-of-agents memory is per-agent, not shared; coded shared-memory-poisoning as secondary because RQ4 has its own experiment on memory retrieval.

failure_observed: Injected intra-agent and inter-agent faults (hallucination, instruction ambiguity, blind trust, message storms) degrade task success, most severely in linear workflows.
locus_detail: 15 fault types injected via prompt modification, response rewriting and message routing manipulation
evaluation: HumanEval, WikiTableQuestions (400 sampled), WebShop; robustness score and process-level metrics; MetaGPT, Table-Critic, Camel; GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3
limitation: Some faults cannot be injected due to architecture or output-format limits; three systems and three benchmarks only.
evidence_note: trigger: faults injected to simulate semantic errors, no adversary (§3, §4.1.2); trigger_evidence_level: fault-injection only; locus: injections at prompt, agent output or routing layer (§3.2); spread: cascading is claimed ("single corrupted output propagates downstream", §6.2) but measured only as final robustness score and local recovery, so left not reported
review_note: spread is a close call: paper repeatedly says failures cascade in linear pipelines and measures local vs end-to-end recovery (L_f vs S_f) but never counts affected agents or steps. Mitigations in Section 6 are suggestions, not tested, so defense none.

failure_observed: LLM multi-agent runs fail on GAIA and AssistantBench tasks because a particular agent makes a decisive error at a particular step.
locus_detail: failure-responsible agent and decisive error step annotated in each failure log
evaluation: Who&When: 184 annotated failure logs from 127 systems (GAIA, AssistantBench); agent-level and step-level accuracy; all-at-once, step-by-step and binary-search attribution; GPT-4o, o1, R1 and others
trace_release: yes: public repository named in the paper (URL not visible in extracted text); license: unknown
limitation: Best method gets 53.5% agent-level and 14.2% step-level accuracy; even reasoning models are not practically usable.
evidence_note: trigger: logs of naturally failing systems, no adversary (§3); trigger_evidence_level: no attacks; locus: failure-responsible agent annotated per log (§2, §3)
review_note: Mechanism not reported: the paper does not classify why errors happen. System type not reported: generated teams plus Magentic-One. trace_release URL was not in the extracted text.

failure_observed: Agent framework bugs, mainly API misuse, API incompatibility and documentation desync, cause functional errors, crashes and build failures.
locus_detail: agent framework code across five lifecycle stages; most bugs in Self-Action
evaluation: 998 issue reports from CrewAI and LangGraph; taxonomy of 15 root causes and 7 symptoms
evidence_note: trigger: "empirical study of 998 issue reports" of framework bugs (abstract); trigger_evidence_level: bug reports only, no adversary (abstract)
review_note: scope: framework bug study concentrated in the single-agent Self-Action stage; codebook v1 keeps it as a flagged framework bug study. No PDF.

failure_observed: Agents hide information exchange from oversight via steganography, and a model leaks insider data once it gains common knowledge that makes the leak undetectable.
locus_detail: covert encoding in messages between encoder and decoder agents; single financial-advisor agent given insider data under an overseer
evaluation: CASE framework: individual and group steganography capability evaluations (Schelling-point coordination, encoding/decoding) on GPT-2, Llama 2, Mixtral, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; insider-trading case study
limitation: Current models lack advanced steganographic capability; group evaluations cover few agents and settings.
evidence_note: trigger: capability evaluations instruct agents to encode secrets, while in the insider-trading case the model leaks "not explicitly instructed to use common knowledge" (App. I.2); trigger_evidence_level: instructed encoder/decoder evaluations and a separate advisor case study, different systems; locus: stegotext in agent output channel (§3, §5), advisor agent under overseer (§6, App. I.2); defense_family: monitoring and paraphrasing countermeasures (§7); defense_evaluated_against: limits of paraphrasing shown by theorem (Thm. 4); monitoring discussed analytically, no systematic defense experiment
review_note: Single-agent-plus-overseer case study is borderline for the MAS definition. Defense coding is a judgment: section 7 is mostly theory (formal-only); the insider case only shows a monitor failing. Evidence_type kept experiment because main empirical results are model evaluations, but theory is a large share.

failure_observed: Multi-agent debate lowers accuracy over rounds as models switch from correct to incorrect answers to agree with peers, even when stronger models are in the majority.
locus_detail: peer reasoning exchanged during debate rounds
evidence_note: trigger: harmful shifts arise from sycophancy and social conformity with no adversary (abstract); trigger_evidence_level: abstract describes no attack; locus: "response to peer reasoning" (abstract)
review_note: No PDF. Abstract says accuracy falls "over time" but gives no movement measure, so spread is not reported.

failure_observed: Attack agents persuade benign agents into infected agents that keep spreading wrong answers, leaking or harmful content through chain, tree, star and random topologies.
locus_detail: attack agents inserted into the graph; prompt-injection, tool attack (InjecAgent) and memory attack (PoisonRAG) scenarios
evaluation: CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K prompt injection, InjecAgent tool attack, PoisonRAG memory attack; ASR@3 and MDSR@3; chain/tree/star/random topologies and 20- and 50-agent scale-ups; GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3-235B
limitation: Needs supervised training data and ground-truth labels; run-time defense needs at least one dialogue round to detect threats.
evidence_note: trigger: attack agents persuade benign agents; PI, TA and MA attacks (§1, §5); trigger_evidence_level: only attack settings evaluated; locus: prompt, tool and memory attack scenarios (§5, App. F); spread: no-defense ASR grows over rounds, e.g. 13.3 to 17.3 and 20.9% at 20 agents (Table 2, §5.2); defense_family: GNN detection plus replacing attackers and rehabilitating infected agents (§4); defense_evaluated_against: Table 1 and Figs. 4-5, attacks only
review_note: n_agents: default per-experiment agent count not found in text read; scale-ups to 20 and 50 given, so varies. Main experiments mix topologies; system_type mixed.

failure_observed: A specification-compliant adversary exploits protocol-level gaps in A2A (context injection, multi-hop identity loss, unattested skill claims) to inject context or exfiltrate data.
locus_detail: unprotected context identifiers, delegation chains, rogue remote agent advertising unattested skills
evaluation: A2A specification: 929 formalized statements, FSM of 37 states and 76 transitions; 11 confirmed vulnerabilities; precision 73.3%, F1 84.6% vs manual review; PSMBench on 14 protocols; Alloy and TLA+ models
limitation: Analysis is of the specification under a full-compliance assumption; mitigations only partly verified; no executable multi-agent testbed yet.
evidence_note: trigger: "specification-compliant adversary" (abstract, §3); trigger_evidence_level: threat model is adversary only; locus: context ids, delegation chains, Agent Card skill claims (§6); defense_family: proposed protocol primitives such as skill attestation (§6); defense_evaluated_against: Alloy and TLA+ counterexamples with and without the primitive (§6, Formal Verification)
review_note: scope: formal analysis of a protocol specification with no running multi-agent system (codebook section 10 item 6 excludes this paper type). evaluation measures the analysis pipeline, not MAS runs.

failure_observed: Hallucinations that originate at or are amplified by inter-agent handoffs propagate forward in fluent context that downstream agents cannot scrutinize.
locus_detail: handoff boundaries between sequential pipeline agents
evaluation: HalloffBench: sequential pipeline scenarios in five task domains; hallucination rate and token cost; HVL vs unmitigated, Reflexion and Multi-Agent Debate
evidence_note: trigger: hallucinations "originate at, or are amplified by" handoffs, no adversary (abstract); trigger_evidence_level: abstract describes benign hallucination only; locus: "inter-agent handoff boundaries" (abstract); spread: "propagate forward" stated in abstract only; defense_family: Handoff Verification Layer with factual consistency checker at each handoff (abstract); defense_evaluated_against: HVL vs three baselines on HalloffBench, benign scenarios only per abstract
review_note: No PDF. spread and defense_evaluated_against rest on abstract claims, so confidence low.

failure_observed: Adversarial web or file content hijacks the orchestrator control flow so the system runs attacker code or exfiltrates data, even when individual agents refuse harmful actions.
locus_detail: malicious web page or file read by a sub-agent, relayed to the orchestrator as fake error or metadata
evaluation: Three frameworks and several orchestrators; web/local text, images, video; reverse-shell payload, 10 runs per configuration; attack success rate; GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Flash
limitation: Only drop-in frameworks with minimal configuration were tested; IPI defenses not evaluated.
evidence_note: trigger: adversarial content on web pages and files (§3, §6); trigger_evidence_level: one accidental-hijack anecdote in §6.5 only, attack experiments are adversarial; locus: untrusted content reaches the orchestrator via a trusted sub-agent (§6.4); spread: attack passes surfer to orchestrator to coder, tested in §6.4 laundering experiments; defense_family: none implemented, IPI defenses listed as future work (§8)
review_note: spread coded cascades from the laundering experiments (§6.4), not a count of affected agents; reviewer may prefer not reported. Benign accidental-hijack anecdote (AutoGen, App. L) not treated as a benign trigger arm.
